query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of 5 at.% titanium (Ti) to the refractory high-entropy alloy NbMoTaW will improve room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance while maintaining excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C.
generation.intervention: Addition of 5 at.% titanium (Ti) to form a refractory high-entropy alloy with composition NbMoTaWTi
generation.conditions: Arc melting and drop casting, followed by heat treatment at 1200 °C for 24 hours
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a stable BCC solid solution with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution
generation.mechanism: The addition of Ti is expected to improve room-temperature ductility by reducing the Peierls stress and promoting dislocation mobility, while maintaining high-temperature mechanical performance due to the preservation of the BCC structure. The enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution are anticipated to improve irradiation tolerance by facilitating self-healing and reducing irradiation-induced defects
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved room-temperature ductility (> 10% elongation) and irradiation tolerance (reduced blistering and amorphization) compared to untreated NbMoTaW, while maintaining excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C
generation.boundary: Temperature range: 20-1600 °C, irradiation conditions: helium implantation
generation.uncertainty: The effect of Ti on the BCC structure and high-temperature properties is not well-established, and further studies are needed to optimize the heat treatment conditions

falsification_experiment.design: Tensile testing and irradiation experiments on NbMoTaW with and without Ti addition
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of Ti does not improve room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, or if it degrades the high-temperature mechanical properties, the hypothesis is falsified
